links.note: 1161: she would hide the sickness, but it rises like spring water for those who bale it out (இறைப்பவர்க்கு ஊற்றுநீர் போல மிகும்). 396: a well in sand wells up as far as it is dug, and understanding as far as one learns (தொட்டனைத்து ஊறும்). The same figure of water that increases the more it is drawn serves learning in one verse and an unconcealable pain in the other.

Both open with the same words, மறைப்பேன்மன் ('I would hide it'), and both say the attempt fails: in 1161 the pain rises like spring water under baling, in 1253 desire shows itself without her intending it, like a sneeze (குறிப்பின்றித் தும்மல்போல்). Read together, one figure says concealment makes it grow and the other that it escapes her will altogether.

1162: she cannot hide the sickness, and telling it to the one who caused it brings shame (உரைத்தலும் நாணுத் தரும்). 1200: she tells her heart that it means to tell its pain to one who is not close (உறாஅர்க்கு உறுநோய் உரைப்பாய்) and might as well fill up the sea. Parimelazhagar reads both as about sending him word; 1200 adds futility to the shame that 1162 gives as the obstacle.

Both use the carrying pole (கா). In 1196 love is painful on one end only and sweet when it is on both ends, the two lovers. In 1163 the pole is her own life (உயிர் காவா) and the two loads are love and shame hanging inside a body that cannot bear them, so the figure of balance turns from two people to two forces within one.

1163 states the deadlock: love and shame hang balanced from her life within a body that cannot bear them (நோனா உடம்பின்). 1247 is her attempt to end it: she tells her heart to let go either desire or shame, since she cannot bear the two (யானோ பொறேன் இவ்விரண்டு).

1017: those ruled by shame give up life for shame and do not give up shame for life (நாணால் உயிரைத் துறப்பர்). 1163 shows that ranking from inside: she drops neither love nor shame, and it is her life, the pole (உயிர் காவா), that takes the strain; Parimelazhagar adds that the life will snap.

1134 (the man): the fierce flood of love carries off the raft called shame and manliness (காமக் கடும்புனல் ... புணை). 1164 (the woman): the sea of love is there, and the safe raft to swim it is not (ஏமப் புணை மன்னும் இல்). The same figure of love as water and restraint or help as a raft is used by each lover, he losing his raft and she never having one.

Both use the compound ஏமப்புணை, 'raft of safety'. In 306 the raft is one's own people (இனமென்னும் ஏமப்புணை), which anger burns; in 1164 there is no such raft for the sea of love, and Parimelazhagar takes her to mean that the friend has not become one. In both the raft stands for people one relies on.

10: the great sea of birth is swum by those who reach the Lord's feet and not by others (பிறவிப் பெருங்கடல் நீந்துவர்); Parimelazhagar supplies the feet as the raft. 1164: the sea of love exists and the raft to swim it does not (அது நீந்தும் ஏமப்புணை). The same structure of a sea crossed only with a support appears in the first chapter and in a separated woman's complaint.

Both argue from the nearer case to the farther with a question. 188: those who spread even the faults of their intimates, what would they do to strangers (என்னைகொல் ஏதிலார் மாட்டு)? 1165: those who can bring grief within friendship (நட்பினுள்), what would they be in enmity (துப்பின் எவனாவர்)?

1165: she asks what those who bring grief in friendship would do as enemies; Parimelazhagar says this is aimed, in a sulk, at the friend who has not sent a message. 805 advises that when friends do something hurtful (நோதக்க நட்டார் செயின்) it should be understood as folly or as great intimacy. 805 offers the charitable reading that her question refuses.

1137 speaks of suffering a love like the sea (கடலன்ன காமம் உழந்தும்) and praises womanhood that still does not mount the palmyra horse. 1166 uses the sea twice over: love's pleasure is a sea, and when it afflicts (அடுங்கால்) the pain is greater than that. The sea is the book's measure for love, and 1166 says the measure is exceeded.

629: one who does not crave the pleasure within pleasure does not come to pain within pain (இன்பத்துள் இன்பம் விழையாதான்). 1166: the pleasure of love is a sea and its pain when it afflicts is larger still (துன்பம் அதனிற் பெரிது). The woman's experience fits the link between relishing pleasure and suffering pain that 629 states as a rule in the Book of Wealth.

1164 says the sea of love exists and there is no raft to swim it. 1167 continues the figure: she has swum the fierce flood (காமக் கடும்புனல் நீந்தி) and sees no shore (கரை காணேன்), and at midnight there is only herself. The second verse turns the missing raft into an actual, endless swim.

Both lovers are awake at midnight, with the same word யாமத்தும். The man in 1136 says his eyes will not close and even at midnight he thinks of mounting the palmyra horse; the woman in 1167 says that even at midnight she alone is there (யானே உளேன்), swimming without sight of shore. Sleeplessness in the dead of night is given to both sides.

1168: the night has put all living beings to sleep and, she says with pity (அளித்து), has no companion but her. 1222: she tells the evening it looks sad-eyed (புன்கண்ணை) and asks whether its partner is as hard as hers. In both she treats a time of day as a fellow sufferer and puts her own state onto it; Parimelazhagar says as much of 1222.

1169: the nights that pass so long these days (நெடிய கழியும் இரா) are crueller than the cruel one's cruelty. 1269: for those who pine with a set day of return in mind, one day passes like seven (ஒருநாள் எழுநாள்போல்). Both say that time stretches for the one who waits.

1169: in separation the long nights are crueller than the man himself. 1329: the man, pleading with her as she sulks, wishes the night would lengthen (நீடுக மன்னோ இரா). The length of the night is a torment or a wish depending on whether the lover is present; Parimelazhagar notes at 1169 that the nights were short in the days of union.

Both use the phrase கொடியார் கொடுமை, 'the cruelty of the cruel one', for the absent man. In 1235 her shoulders, their old beauty faded, declare it; in 1169 she uses it as the measure the long nights exceed (கொடுமையின் தாம் கொடிய). 1169 moves the charge of cruelty from the man to the time itself.

1170: if her eyes could go where he is as her heart does (உள்ளம்போன்று உள்வழிச் செல்கிற்பின்), they would not be swimming in a flood of tears. 1244 turns the wish into a request: heart, take the eyes along when you go (கண்ணும் கொளச்சேறி), for they consume her in wanting to see him. Both rest on the idea that the heart can travel to him and the eyes cannot.

In 1167 she herself swims the fierce flood of love and sees no shore; in 1170 it is her eyes that swim in flood water (வெள்ளநீர் நீந்தல), which is her tears. The chapter's water figure for love ends as literal water in the eyes.

1091 (the man): her kohl-lined eyes hold two looks, one that gives the sickness and one that is its cure (நோய்நோக்கு ... மருந்து). 1171 (the woman): her own eyes showed him to her and so she came to know an unabating sickness (தண்டாநோய்), and she asks why they weep. Eyes are the source of love's sickness in both, the other's eyes for the man and her own for the woman, and only his verse has a cure.

1171: she asks why her eyes weep, since they showed him to her (தாம் காட்ட யாம் கண்டது). 1244: the eyes consume her in their wish to see him (அவர்க்காணல் உற்று). In both she speaks of her eyes as agents apart from herself, with wants of their own that she pays for.

792: the friendship of one who does not take it after examining again and again ends in grief that kills him (ஆய்ந்தாய்ந்து கொள்ளாதான் கேண்மை). 1172, on Parimelazhagar's reading: the eyes looked that day without examining and understanding what would follow (தெரிந்துணரா நோக்கிய) and now suffer. The rule about forming ties without scrutiny is applied to a look. Manakkudavar reads the first phrase differently, as having looked with knowledge.

535: one who slipped by not guarding beforehand will grieve afterwards over his own error (முன்னுறக் காவாது ... பின்னூறு இரங்கிவிடும்). 1172: the eyes that looked without foresight now toil in misery (பைதல் உழப்பது). Parimelazhagar's comment on 1172 uses the same terms, that those who do not guard against what is coming can only bear it when it arrives.

1173: the eyes looked hastily of themselves (கதுமெனத் தாம் நோக்கி) and now weep of themselves, which is laughable. 435: the life of one who does not guard before a fault comes is destroyed like straw before fire (வருமுன்னர்க் காவாதான்). Parimelazhagar explains the laughter in 1173 with that same phrase: it is laughable to those who guard before it comes.

1140: the ignorant laugh where she can see it (நகுப அறிவில்லார்), because they have not suffered what she has. 1173: she finds her own eyes' plight fit to be laughed at (நகத்தக்கது உடைத்து). Laughter at a lover's suffering comes from outsiders in one verse and from the sufferer herself in the other.

320: all pain falls on those who caused pain (நோயெல்லாம் நோய்செய்தார் மேலவாம்). 1174: the eyes that fixed an inescapable sickness in her (உய்வில்நோய் என்கண் நிறுத்து) have themselves dried up and cannot weep. Parimelazhagar reads 1174 in these terms: having done her harm first, harm came to them of itself.

319: if you do hurt to others in the forenoon, hurt comes to you in the afternoon of itself (தாமே வரும்). 1175: the eyes that made her a sickness the sea cannot hold now cannot sleep and toil in misery (படலாற்றா பைதல் உழக்கும்). Manakkudavar states the connection, saying the verse shows harm coming to those who did harm to another.

1166 says love's pain, when it afflicts, is greater than the sea (அதனிற் பெரிது). 1175 repeats the measure as an epithet, a love-sickness the sea cannot hold (கடலாற்றாக் காமநோய்), and goes on to assign blame for it to her eyes.

1173 finds it laughable that the eyes looked of themselves and weep of themselves. 1176 goes a step further: it is sweet (ஓஒ இனிதே) that the eyes which gave her this sickness have fallen into it too (தாஅம் இதற்பட்டது). The sequence moves from mockery of her eyes to satisfaction at their suffering.

1174 reports that the eyes have dried up and cannot weep (நீருலந்த). 1177 wishes exactly that on them: may the eyes that longed and melted to see him suffer on until their inner water is gone (உள்நீர் அறுக). What one verse states as their condition the other pronounces as a curse.

The two verses share most of their wording. 1178: there is one who desired without cherishing (பேணாது பெட்டார்), and her eyes cannot be at peace without seeing him (காணாது அமைவில கண்). 1283: though he disregards her and does what pleases him (பேணாது பெட்பவே செய்யினும்), her eyes will not rest without seeing her husband. Both set his lack of care against the eyes' need to see him; Manakkudavar reads the opening of 1178 differently, as a question about desiring what should not be desired.

1179: when he does not come the eyes do not sleep, and when he comes they do not sleep (வாராக்கால் துஞ்சா வரின் துஞ்சா). 1295: the heart fears not having him and, having him, fears parting (பெறாஅமை அஞ்சும் பெறின் பிரிவு அஞ்சும்). The same two-sided bind is said of the eyes and of the heart, and Parimelazhagar explains 1179 by the fear of parting that 1295 names.

1152: once his mere look was a pleasure, and now union itself holds the pain of fearing separation (பிரிவஞ்சும் புன்கண் உடைத்தால் புணர்வு). 1179 gives the bodily result: her eyes do not sleep even when he has come. 1152 supplies the reason for the second half of 1179.

Both use the beaten drum (அறைபறை) for giving away a secret (மறை). In 1076 the base are like the drum because they carry whatever secret they hear to others. In 1180 her own eyes are the drum, so the town easily gets the secret in her heart. The figure for a vice in the Book of Wealth becomes a figure for a lover's helplessness.

1180 (the woman): the town can easily learn the secret of those whose eyes are beaten drums. 1271 (the man): though she hides it, her kohl-lined eyes go beyond her control (கரப்பினும் கையிகந்து) and have something to tell. Both lovers say her eyes disclose what she means to conceal.

71: is there a bolt that can shut in love? The small tears of the loving will proclaim it (புன்கணீர் பூசல் தரும்). 1180: her eyes are beaten drums and the town easily learns her secret. The Book of Virtue says of அன்பு in general what the woman says of her own love: the eyes publish it.
